title: The Supreme Court Just Saved Birthright Citizenship. No Community Had More at Stake Than Indian Americans.
excerpt: With green card backlogs stretching past a century, tens of thousands of Indian families in the U.S. faced losing their children's citizenship. The 6-3 ruling shuts that door.
body:
The U.S. Supreme Court has definitively upheld birthright citizenship, striking down President Donald Trump's executive order that sought to deny automatic citizenship to children born in America to non-citizen parents. The 6-3 ruling, delivered on the eve of America's 250th birthday, carries particular weight for the roughly 4.5 million Indian Americans and hundreds of thousands of Indian families navigating the country's labyrinthine immigration system.

Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority, was unambiguous: "Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community. The framers of the Fourteenth Amendment extended that promise to every free-born person in this land. We keep that promise today."

## Why This Ruling Hits Home for Indian Families

No immigrant community in America lives under the shadow of visa uncertainty quite like Indians do. With green card backlogs stretching past 100 years for Indian-born applicants, and H-1B renewals perpetually at risk, tens of thousands of Indian families spend decades in the U.S. without permanent status. Their children, born on American soil, have until now been unambiguously American.

Trump's September 2025 executive order attempted to change that, proposing to strip citizenship from children born to parents present in the country on temporary visas or without authorization. For Indian families on H-1B, L-1, or student visas — where a child can be born, raised, and schooled entirely in America while parents wait decades for a green card — the threat was existential.

"Indian and South Asian immigrant families are among those most directly threatened by Trump's executive order," said Chintan Patel, Executive Director of Indian American Impact, in a statement following the ruling. "Communities navigating long visa backlogs and uncertain immigration timelines, where children are often born here long before their parents have a clear path to permanence."



> **"Chief Justice John Roberts, writing for the majority, was unambiguous: "Citizenship, then and now, was the right to have rights — to freely participate in our political community."**


## The Numbers Tell the Story

Had the executive order survived judicial scrutiny, an estimated 4.8 million future U.S.-born children would have been stripped of citizenship by 2045, and 12.8 million by 2075, according to projections from the Migration Policy Institute cited in court filings. Indians, who account for over 70% of all approved H-1B petitions annually, would have borne a disproportionate share of that impact.


![President Donald Trump — Photo: Wikimedia Commons](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/1/13/Official_Presidential_Portrait_of_President_Donald_J._Trump_%282025%29_%28cropped%29%282%29.jpg)


The ruling comes amid a broader assault on immigration pathways that Indian professionals depend on. In the same Supreme Court term, the justices stripped Temporary Protected Status from hundreds of thousands of Haitians and Syrians, made it easier to deny entry to green card holders, and expanded the administration's deportation powers.

## A Personal Victory

Trisha Prabhu, a Yale Law student and Indian American, wrote in a USA Today op-ed that the ruling struck at something deeply personal. "Anti-Indian sentiment has reached a fever pitch," she wrote, citing Vivek Ramaswamy's account of being told to go "back to India" despite being born and raised in Cincinnati.

"At a moment when the country expresses its distaste for the Indian part of our identity, we also have had to contend with attacks on the American part," Prabhu wrote. "But now, the Supreme Court stood up. It stood up for me."

## What's Next

The ruling settles the constitutional question but does not end the political fight. Trump responded on Truth Social that the decision was "too bad for our country," and conservative legal scholars have called it a "catastrophic loss." Justice Clarence Thomas, in a scathing dissent, argued the majority had "devalued American citizenship."

Congress could still pass legislation addressing birth tourism or narrowing certain eligibility criteria, and the administration retains its powers over visas, border enforcement, and removals. The H-1B program itself remains under pressure: a separate federal judge recently struck down Trump's $100,000 H-1B fee as an unlawful tax, though the White House has vowed to appeal.

For now, however, the constitutional floor holds. Children born in America to Indian parents on work visas, student visas, or even without documentation are Americans — full stop. As the country marks 250 years since its founding, the court has reaffirmed the promise that drew many of those families across the world in the first place.

*Sources: Reuters, USA Today, The Indian Eye, North Jersey Media Group, Associated Press*
